title: craving
hookLine: craving — wanting things to be other than they are

lines: THE GAP BETWEEN IS AND WANT.
cards: You're in a slow line at the grocery store. The person ahead is paying in coins. Counting them.
Out loud. For a lot of people, something happens in the body. The jaw tightens.
The weight shifts. A little voice starts narrating: why is this line always the slow one. Now here's the odd thing.
The line is just a line. It isn't hurting anyone. What hurts, looked at closely, is the gap between the line that is and the line that's wanted.

teach.b: The second noble truth is about where dukkha comes from. In Pali it's samudaya, arising, origin. And the Buddha's answer is one word: tanha.
It literally means thirst. Not a polite preference. Thirst.

The dry-mouthed, leaning-forward kind that makes you reach before you think. In the first sermon he names three thirsts. The thirst for pleasant things: the next bite, the next scroll, the next thing to buy.
The thirst to be something: to be seen, to be right, to last. And the thirst not to be: to make something go away, to disappear from a feeling, to wish this moment weren't happening.

teach.h: WANTING MORE, TO BE, NOT TO BE.
teach.b: Some teachers read that third thirst widely: wanting something gone is a thirst too. On that reading, the grocery line is thirst of the third kind. Here's a careful point.

Buddhism doesn't say every wish is a problem. Teachers use a different Pali word, chanda, for a wish or will that can be wholesome: the wish to be kind, the intention to practice, the will to get up and help someone.
What the second truth names is the grasping kind. The kind that insists: this should be different, right now, or I can't be okay. So letting go of craving doesn't mean loving people less.
The Buddha taught families how to care for each other. The trouble is the grip, not the care. And here's why it's hopeful, not harsh.
If the wobble came from the world, you'd be stuck. You can't make every line fast. But if it comes from the thirst, there's something you can actually work with.
The thirst is closer to home.

how: Buddhists learn the second noble truth as the arising of dukkha from craving, and in meditation practice noticing wanting and aversion as they come up, without acting on them right away.

games.q: what's inside the truth — tap the pairs.
p: a wish that can be wholesome
the thirst not to be here

s: Buddhism says every desire is bad
teachers distinguish grasping craving from wholesome wishes like the will to be kind.
the dry-mouthed, reaching kind. that's the picture.
letting go of craving means loving your family less
the trouble is the grip, not the care. the Buddha taught families how to look after each other.

games.q: you're stuck in a slow line and getting furious. according to the second truth, where does the wobble come from?
o: the gap between the line that is and the line you want.
games.why: the second truth points at tanha, the thirst. the line is just a line; the wanting it to be different is where the wobble starts.

practice: The bell gives you about forty-five seconds. Find something you want right now. Food, a message, for this lesson to end.
Anything. Feel where the wanting lives in your body: the chest, the hands, the jaw. Don't get rid of it, and don't follow it.
Just notice that it's a feeling, and that it's thirsty, and keep breathing beside it.

wordCard.voice: Tanha. Thirst: the second truth's answer to where dukkha comes from, wanting things to be other than they are. Ninth word.

orig.note: Pali: thirst, craving. Sanskrit tṛṣṇā. The origin (samudaya) of dukkha in the second noble truth.

carryVoice: Your line: the wanting is the wobble. The line was only ever a line. Day nine, done.

sources.ref: Dhammacakkappavattana Sutta (Samyutta Nikaya 56.11): the second truth and the three kinds of craving
